newsitem.title: USA: Wells shares up after early fall on Q2.
newsitem.headline: Wells shares up after early fall on Q2.

text.p: Wells Fargo and Co's shares rose in afternoon trade, erasing earlier losses that followed the release of lower second quarter results that were in line with the bank's earnings forecast made last week.

"Most of the news was already reflected in the stock price last week," said Stephen Biggar, analyst with S&P Equity Group, referring to the announcement last week that earnings would be nearly one-third below estimates due to troubles integrating First Interstate, which Wells acquired last year.
"The results were not much worse than they warned. They were basically in the range," said Biggar.
Wells' warning last week sent its shares tumbling 6.6 percent in heavy trade last Wednesday. Today, Wells shares rose 2-5/16 to 267-13/16 after earlier dipping to $260-3/8.
Wells chairman Paul Hazen said he was disappointed with the second quarter earnings of $2.49 a share or $228 million versus $363 million or $3.61 a share a year ago.

Wells cited an increase in operating losses due to various operational and back-office issues related to the First Interstate integration, including clearing accounts with other banks. The losses totalled $180 million in the second quarter, compared with first quarter 1997 losses of $42 million.

Wells said there was incorrect posting of some customer deposits several months ago in which deposits never made it to the accounts. Wells credited the customers but was unable in some cases to find the deposits and had to write them off.
"Clearly, they have had challenges and it's disappointing to see there's still some integration issues surfacing," said Alex. Brown analyst Joseph Morford.
"The trouble at Wells is certainly playing into the hands of competing community banks and some larger banks like BankAmerica (Corp )," he said.
Analysts were also disappointed by sluggish revenues.
"Top line revenues continued to decline in the quarter, but that was somewhat offset by improvement in the fee area,' said Morford.
One analyst attributed Wells' troubles to the hostile nature of the merger.

"I have a feeling it has a lot to with the the fact it was a hostile merger. A lot of top managers left Interstate when the deal closed. At this stage, you have to wonder if it would have gone a lot more smoothly had they stuck around," the analyst said.
